title: [Chapitre] II. Réalisations topologiques des réseaux : notes manuscrites (06/06/1986).

deep.reconstruction:
Setting (from pp. 7-9): a 'ficelle' (string) is F=(X,{A,B}), a space X with two distinguished 'lieux' A, B, its extremities. A lieu is a cut-locus; it need not be a point, since the previous lemma says 'OPS A,B,C,D réduits à des points'. Cutting F along an interior lieu C gives two sub-strings F_{A,C} and F_{B,C}, with X = X_{a,c} ⊔_c X_{c,b}. Every lieu of a piece is a lieu of F. The lemma on p.7: for distinct interior lieux C, D, D is a lieu of F_{B,C} iff C is a lieu of F_{A,D}. Swapping A and B gives: D is a lieu of F_{A,C} iff C is a lieu of F_{B,D}.

This page:
(1) Definition of disjoint lieux, a symmetric relation. If C or D is an extremity, disjoint just means C≠D. If both are interior, disjoint means C≠D and D is a lieu of F_{A,C} or of F_{B,C}. By the lemma this is equivalent to C being a lieu of F_{B,D} or of F_{A,D}, which is why the relation is symmetric. The definition is needed because lieux are not points: two distinct lieux can overlap, and then neither lies in a piece cut out by the other.
(2) An oriented string is a string with one extremity fixed as origin or(F); the other is ex(F).
(3) Claimed equivalence of categories. On one side: oriented strings with two disjoint interior lieux. On the other: 'suites' (F1,F2,F3,h21,h32) of oriented strings with gluing isomorphisms h21: ex(F1)≅or(F2) and h32: ex(F2)≅or(F3). One direction cuts at the two lieux; the other concatenates by gluing along the isomorphisms. This is the formal statement that a 1-dimensional 'interval' object is determined by its pieces and gluing data (cutting and pasting).
(4) The order on lieux of an oriented string F=(X,(A,B)). Set F_C = the set of lieux of F_{A,C} for C≠A,B, F_A={A}, F_B = all lieux. Define C≤D iff F_C⊂F_D, equivalently C∈F_D.

On the next page this order is axiomatised: least and greatest elements α≠β; the sets of elements above x (resp. below x) are filtering; density (if x<y there is z with x<z<y); distinct disjoint lieux are comparable. The upshot is an order-theoretic description of the lieux of a string, a partial order that is total on disjoint families, analogous to the classical order characterisations of the arc. The purpose is the 1-dimensional foundations for 'topological realizations of networks' (graphs/maps): strings are the edges, and concatenation along endpoint identifications is the basic gluing.
errors: Minor gap: the equivalence C≤D ⇔ C∈F_D uses transitivity of being a lieu (a lieu of F_{A,C} with C a lieu of F_{A,D} is a lieu of F_{A,D}), which follows from the decomposition in the p.7 lemma but is not spelled out.

Minor gap: functoriality and essential surjectivity of the claimed equivalence are only asserted. The gluing direction needs that the glued space with the images of the end lieux is again a string whose lieux are those of the pieces; this is not proved on this page.
The edge cases of the 'disjoint' definition when one lieu is an extremity are by convention.

ideas.what: Axiomatic 'string' (ficelle) with cut-loci (lieux), cutting along a lieu into two sub-strings
ideas.modern_name: Axiomatic arc / interval object; cut points of continua (Moore's characterisation of the arc)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Classical continuum theory (R.L. Moore, Kuratowski, Whyburn); order characterisations of the line (Cantor, Veblen)

ideas.what: Disjointness of lieux as a symmetric relation, made necessary by lieux possibly being thick (overlapping) subsets
ideas.modern_name: Disjoint/non-overlapping cut sets; overlapping closed intervals

ideas.what: Equivalence: oriented strings with two disjoint interior lieux ≃ triples of oriented strings with endpoint gluing isomorphisms
ideas.modern_name: Concatenation/cut-and-paste of intervals; composition of paths (Moore paths, interval as monoid/operad); descent for 1-dimensional pieces

ideas.what: Partial order on lieux of an oriented string via F_C ⊂ F_D, leading (next page) to bounded, filtering, dense order axioms
ideas.modern_name: Order characterisation of the interval / betweenness on an arc

missed.claim: The page is part of an unpublished attempt to found a combinatorial/tame 1-dimensional topology: 'ficelles' with possibly non-point 'lieux', cutting and gluing equivalences, and an order structure. It serves topological realization of 'réseaux', presumably related to his dessins/maps programme. The general framework with thick cut-loci and categorical gluing equivalences was not developed in print. The individual statements here are routine.
missed.quote: La catégorie des ficelles orientées munies de deux lieux disjoints, est équivalente à celle des suites (F_1, F_2, F_3, h_{21}, h_{32})
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Mainly historical: it documents how Grothendieck intended to set up 'tame topology' foundations for graphs/maps (cf. Esquisse d'un programme) axiomatically and categorically. No new theorem for specialists.

deep.surprise_reason: Careful but elementary foundational material: definitions of disjoint lieux, oriented strings, a cut/glue category equivalence and an order on lieux. Historically interesting as part of unpublished 1986 tame-topology foundations, but mathematically classical.
transcription_corrections: Throughout this page 'Lignes'/'ligne' should read 'Lieux'/'lieu' (e.g. 'Lieux disjoints', 'D est un lieu de F_{A,C}'), consistent with pp. 7 and 9.
Bottom-left marginal note, '(si C ≠ A,B ; ={A} si C=A ; =F si C=B)', is written in the margin as an insertion.
Header '8 C, D (relation symétrique)' is correct: symmetry refers to the disjointness relation.
Last line likely reads 'Cela signifie que C ∈ F_D' ('aussi' uncertain).
